title: White Dwarfs, Degenerate Matter & Chandrasekhar Limit
text:
When a star exhausts nuclear fuel, gravitational collapse compresses matter to extreme densities \(\rho \gtrsim 10^6\text{ g/cm}^3\). In this regime, electrons fill all available phase space cells \((h^3)\) up to the Fermi momentum \(p_F\): \[n_e = \frac{8\pi}{h^3} \int_0^{p_F} p^2 dp = \frac{8\pi}{3h^3} p_F^3 \implies p_F = \left( \frac{3h^3 n_e}{8\pi} \right)^{1/3}\]


The kinetic energy is \(E = p^2 / 2m_e\). The resulting electron degeneracy pressure is: \[P_e = \frac{1}{3} \int_0^{p_F} v p \cdot \frac{8\pi p^2}{h^3} dp = \frac{8\pi}{15 m_e h^3} p_F^5 = \frac{1}{5m_e}\left(\frac{3}{\pi}\right)^{2/3} h^2 n_e^{5/3}\] Since \(n_e = \frac{\rho}{\mu_e m_u}\), this is a polytropic equation of state with index \(n = 3/2\) (\(\gamma = 5/3\)): \[P \propto \rho^{5/3}\]
Solving the Lane-Emden equation for \(n=1.5\) yields the mass-radius relation for non-relativistic white dwarfs: \[R \propto M^{-1/3}\] More massive white dwarfs are physically smaller and denser!

title: White Dwarfs, Degenerate Matter & Chandrasekhar Limit
text:
When a star exhausts nuclear fuel, gravitational collapse compresses matter to extreme densities \(\rho \gtrsim 10^6\text{ g/cm}^3\). In this regime, electrons fill all available phase space cells \((h^3)\) up to the Fermi momentum \(p_F\): \[n_e = \frac{8\pi}{h^3} \int_0^{p_F} p^2 dp = \frac{8\pi}{3h^3} p_F^3 \implies p_F = \left( \frac{3h^3 n_e}{8\pi} \right)^{1/3}\]


The kinetic energy is \(E = p^2 / 2m_e\). The resulting electron degeneracy pressure is: \[P_e = \frac{1}{3} \int_0^{p_F} v p \cdot \frac{8\pi p^2}{h^3} dp = \frac{8\pi}{15 m_e h^3} p_F^5 = \frac{1}{5m_e}\left(\frac{3}{\pi}\right)^{2/3} h^2 n_e^{5/3}\] Since \(n_e = \frac{\rho}{\mu_e m_u}\), this is a polytropic equation of state with index \(n = 3/2\) (\(\gamma = 5/3\)): \[P \propto \rho^{5/3}\]
Solving the Lane-Emden equation for \(n=1.5\) yields the mass-radius relation for non-relativistic white dwarfs: \[R \propto M^{-1/3}\] More massive white dwarfs are physically smaller and denser!

title: White Dwarfs, Degenerate Matter & Chandrasekhar Limit
text:
2. Ultra-Relativistic Degeneracy & The Chandrasekhar Limit
As mass increases, density rises until electrons become relativistic (\(p_F \gg m_e c\)). Then \(v \approx c\), and the energy is \(E \approx pc\): \[P_e = \frac{1}{3} \int_0^{p_F} c p \cdot \frac{8\pi p^2}{h^3} dp = \frac{2\pi c}{3 h^3} p_F^4 = \frac{hc}{4}\left(\frac{3}{\pi}\right)^{1/3} n_e^{4/3} \propto \rho^{4/3}\] This corresponds to a polytrope of index \(n = 3\) (\(\gamma = 4/3\)).
For an \(n=3\) polytrope, the radius cancels out completely in the stellar structure mass integral, producing a unique limiting mass: \[M_{\text{Ch}} = 4\pi \left(\frac{hc}{G}\right)^{3/2} \left(\frac{1}{\mu_e m_u}\right)^2 \omega_3 \approx \frac{5.83}{\mu_e^2} M_\odot\]
For a standard carbon-oxygen white dwarf, \(\mu_e \approx 2\), yielding: \[\boxed{M_{\text{Ch}} \approx 1.44 M_\odot}\]
If the mass of the core exceeds \(M_{\text{Ch}}\), electron degeneracy pressure can never halt gravitational collapse, leading inevitably to a neutron star or black hole.

title: Computational Astrophysics: Polytropes & Interactive HR Diagram
Computational Astrophysics: Polytropes & Interactive HR Diagram
Computational Astrophysics: Polytropes & Interactive HR Diagram
text:
2. Fortran 90: High-Performance Lane-Emden Equation Solver
The Lane-Emden equation governs the dimensionless density profile \(\theta(\xi)\) of self-gravitating polytropic fluid spheres (\(P = K \rho^{1 + 1/n}\)): \[\frac{1}{\xi^2} \frac{d}{d\xi}\left( \xi^2 \frac{d\theta}{d\xi} \right) + \theta^n = 0\]
Boundary conditions at the stellar center (\(\xi = 0\)) are \(\theta(0) = 1\) and \(\theta'(0) = 0\).
! lane_emden.f90
! Compile: gfortran -O3 -std=f2018 lane_emden.f90 -o lane_emden
program solve_lane_emden
    implicit none
    integer, parameter :: dp = kind(1.0d0)
    real(dp) :: xi, theta, phi, dxi, xi_max, n_poly
    real(dp) :: k1_th, k1_ph, k2_th, k2_ph, k3_th, k3_ph, k4_th, k4_ph
    integer :: step, max_steps

    n_poly = 3.0_dp   ! n = 3 (Eddington Standard Model for Relativistic Radiation/Degeneracy)
    dxi = 0.001_dp
    max_steps = 100000

    ! Initial series expansion around xi = 0 to bypass coordinate singularity:
    ! theta(xi) ~ 1 - xi^2 / 6 + n * xi^4 / 120
    xi = 0.001_dp
    theta = 1.0_dp - (xi**2)/6.0_dp + n_poly*(xi**4)/120.0_dp
    phi = -(xi/3.0_dp) + n_poly*(xi**3)/30.0_dp  ! phi = d(theta)/d(xi)

    print '(A, F5.2)', "Solving Lane-Emden equation for polytropic index n = ", n_poly

    do step = 1, max_steps
        if (theta <= 0.0_dp) exit

        ! RK4 Integrator for system: d(theta)/dxi = phi, d(phi)/dxi = -theta^n - 2*phi/xi
        call derivatives(xi, theta, phi, n_poly, k1_th, k1_ph)
        call derivatives(xi + 0.5_dp*dxi, theta + 0.5_dp*dxi*k1_th, phi + 0.5_dp*dxi*k1_ph, n_poly, k2_th, k2_ph)
        call derivatives(xi + 0.5_dp*dxi, theta + 0.5_dp*dxi*k2_th, phi + 0.5_dp*dxi*k2_ph, n_poly, k3_th, k3_ph)
        call derivatives(xi + dxi, theta + dxi*k3_th, phi + dxi*k3_ph, n_poly, k4_th, k4_ph)

        theta = theta + (dxi/6.0_dp)*(k1_th + 2.0_dp*k2_th + 2.0_dp*k3_th + k4_th)
        phi   = phi   + (dxi/6.0_dp)*(k1_ph + 2.0_dp*k2_ph + 2.0_dp*k3_ph + k4_ph)
        xi    = xi + dxi
    end do

    print '(A, F8.4)', "Stellar Surface xi_1 = ", xi
    print '(A, F8.4)', "Surface gradient |d(theta)/dxi| = ", abs(phi)
    print '(A, F8.4)', "Dimensionless Mass Ratio -xi_1^2 * theta'(xi_1) = ", xi**2 * abs(phi)

contains

    subroutine derivatives(x, th, ph, n, dth, dph)
        real(dp), intent(in) :: x, th, ph, n
        real(dp), intent(out) :: dth, dph
        dth = ph
        if (th > 0.0_dp) then
            dph = - (th**n) - (2.0_dp * ph / x)
        else
            dph = 0.0_dp
        end if
    end subroutine derivatives

end program solve_lane_emden

title: Problem Set #1: Stellar Structure & Hydrostatic Equilibrium
text:
Due Date: October 1, 2026 at 12:00 Noon on Quercus.
Name file with your last 3 digits of student ID (e.g. astb23_a1_xxx.pdf).
Follow the 6-step problem-solving protocol (sketch, analytic derivation, units check, calculation, plausibility check, description).




Assuming a simple linear density profile \(\rho(r) = \rho_c (1 - r/R)\), where \(R\) is the stellar radius and \(\rho_c\) is the central density: 1. Find the total mass \(M\) in terms of \(\rho_c\) and \(R\). 2. Express the central density \(\rho_c\) in terms of average density \(\bar{\rho} = 3M / (4\pi R^3)\). 3. Integrate the hydrostatic equilibrium equation \(\frac{dP}{dr} = -\frac{G M(r)\rho(r)}{r^2}\) from the surface (\(P(R) = 0\)) to the center to find the central pressure \(P_c\). 4. Evaluate \(P_c\) for solar values (\(M_\odot = 1.989 \times 10^{30}\text{ kg}, R_\odot = 6.96 \times 10^8\text{ m}\)) and compare with the ideal gas pressure at \(T_c \approx 1.5 \times 10^7\text{ K}\).




From the Virial Theorem for an ideal gas sphere bound by gravity, \(2K + U = 0\): 1. Show that the total energy \(E = K + U = \frac{1}{2}U = -K\). 2. Explain why a star contracting quasi-statically under gravity heats up rather than cools down (negative heat capacity). 3. Estimate the Kelvin-Helmholtz gravitational contraction timescale \(t_{\text{KH}} = \frac{|U|}{2L}\) for the Sun.

title: Interactive Galactic Rotation & Dark Matter Simulation
text:
In a spiral galaxy, the radial gravitational acceleration in the disk midplane (\(z=0\)) balances the centrifugal acceleration for circular orbits: \[\frac{v_c^2(R)}{R} = \left| \frac{\partial \Phi_{\text{tot}}}{\partial R} \right| \implies v_c^2(R) = v_{\text{bulge}}^2(R) + v_{\text{disk}}^2(R) + v_{\text{halo}}^2(R)\]


Modeled as a spherical Plummer potential \(\Phi_b(r) = -\frac{G M_b}{\sqrt{r^2 + b_b^2}}\): \[v_{\text{bulge}}(R) = \sqrt{\frac{G M_b R^2}{(R^2 + b_b^2)^{3/2}}}\]



For an exponential surface density \(\Sigma(R) = \Sigma_0 e^{-R/R_d}\), the circular velocity peaks near \(R \approx 2.2 R_d\) and falls off at large radii: \[v_{\text{disk}}(R) \approx v_{d,\text{max}} \cdot \frac{1.97 (R/R_d)^{1.22}}{[(R/R_d)^{2} + 0.78]^{1.43}}\]



A core radius \(R_c\) and asymptotic velocity \(V_h\): \[\rho_h(R) = \frac{\rho_0}{1 + (R/R_c)^2} \implies v_{\text{halo}}(R) = V_h \sqrt{1 - \frac{R_c}{R}\arctan\left(\frac{R}{R_c}\right)}\]

title: Interactive Galactic Rotation & Dark Matter Simulation
text:
In a spiral galaxy, the radial gravitational acceleration in the disk midplane (\(z=0\)) balances the centrifugal acceleration for circular orbits: \[\frac{v_c^2(R)}{R} = \left| \frac{\partial \Phi_{\text{tot}}}{\partial R} \right| \implies v_c^2(R) = v_{\text{bulge}}^2(R) + v_{\text{disk}}^2(R) + v_{\text{halo}}^2(R)\]


Modeled as a spherical Plummer potential \(\Phi_b(r) = -\frac{G M_b}{\sqrt{r^2 + b_b^2}}\): \[v_{\text{bulge}}(R) = \sqrt{\frac{G M_b R^2}{(R^2 + b_b^2)^{3/2}}}\]



For an exponential surface density \(\Sigma(R) = \Sigma_0 e^{-R/R_d}\), the circular velocity peaks near \(R \approx 2.2 R_d\) and falls off at large radii: \[v_{\text{disk}}(R) \approx v_{d,\text{max}} \cdot \frac{1.97 (R/R_d)^{1.22}}{[(R/R_d)^{2} + 0.78]^{1.43}}\]



A core radius \(R_c\) and asymptotic velocity \(V_h\): \[\rho_h(R) = \frac{\rho_0}{1 + (R/R_c)^2} \implies v_{\text{halo}}(R) = V_h \sqrt{1 - \frac{R_c}{R}\arctan\left(\frac{R}{R_c}\right)}\]

title: Stellar Structure & The Lane-Emden Equation
text:
A spherical star in steady state balances inward gravitational force with outward gas/radiation pressure: \[\boxed{\frac{dP}{dr} = -\frac{G M(r) \rho(r)}{r^2}}\] where the enclosed mass \(M(r)\) satisfies the mass conservation equation: \[\frac{dM}{dr} = 4\pi r^2 \rho(r)\]
Combining these two equations by differentiating \(r^2 \frac{dP}{dr}\): \[\frac{1}{r^2} \frac{d}{dr}\left( \frac{r^2}{\rho} \frac{dP}{dr} \right) = -4\pi G \rho\]

title: Stellar Structure & The Lane-Emden Equation
text:
A spherical star in steady state balances inward gravitational force with outward gas/radiation pressure: \[\boxed{\frac{dP}{dr} = -\frac{G M(r) \rho(r)}{r^2}}\] where the enclosed mass \(M(r)\) satisfies the mass conservation equation: \[\frac{dM}{dr} = 4\pi r^2 \rho(r)\]
Combining these two equations by differentiating \(r^2 \frac{dP}{dr}\): \[\frac{1}{r^2} \frac{d}{dr}\left( \frac{r^2}{\rho} \frac{dP}{dr} \right) = -4\pi G \rho\]

title: Stellar Structure & The Lane-Emden Equation
text:
2. Polytropic Equation of State
To close the structure equation without solving detailed energy transport, we introduce a polytropic relation: \[P = K \rho^\gamma = K \rho^{1 + 1/n}\] where \(n\) is the polytropic index (\(\gamma = 1 + \frac{1}{n}\)): * \(n = 1.5\) (\(\gamma = 5/3\)): Non-relativistic degenerate electron gas (White Dwarfs) or fully convective stars (Red Giants, Sun’s core). * \(n = 3.0\) (\(\gamma = 4/3\)): Relativistic degenerate electron gas (Chandrasekhar mass limit) or radiation-pressure dominated massive stars.

The Dimensionless Lane-Emden Equation
Define dimensionless density \(\theta(\xi)\) and radius \(\xi\): \[\rho(r) = \rho_c \theta^n(\xi), \qquad r = \alpha \xi\] where \(\alpha^2 = \frac{(n+1) K \rho_c^{1/n - 1}}{4\pi G}\).
Substituting into the hydrostatic equation yields the Lane-Emden Equation: \[\boxed{\frac{1}{\xi^2} \frac{d}{d\xi}\left( \xi^2 \frac{d\theta}{d\xi} \right) + \theta^n = 0}\] with boundary conditions at the stellar center (\(\xi = 0\)): \[\theta(0) = 1, \qquad \left. \frac{d\theta}{d\xi} \right|_{\xi=0} = 0\]
The stellar surface \(\xi_1\) is defined where density drops to zero: \(\theta(\xi_1) = 0\).

title: Lectures 21–22: Rotation Curves, Dark Matter & Spiral Arms
text:
In disk galaxies, circular velocity \(v_c(R)\) is governed by radial gravitational equilibrium: \[\frac{v_c^2(R)}{R} = -\frac{\partial \Phi}{\partial R} = \frac{G M(R)}{R^2}\]


If galaxy mass were concentrated solely in the luminous stars and gas (like the solar system), the outer rotation curve would drop as: \[v_c(R) \propto R^{-1/2} \quad (\text{Keplerian falloff})\] However, 21-cm neutral hydrogen (HI) and optical \(H\alpha\) observations show flat rotation curves extending far beyond the optical disk: \[v_c(R) \approx \text{constant} \implies M(R) \propto R\] This necessitates an extended, quasi-spherical Dark Matter Halo with density profile \(\rho(R) \propto R^{-2}\).



Total circular velocity is partitioned into component potentials: \[v_{\text{tot}}^2(R) = v_{\text{bulge}}^2(R) + v_{\text{disk}}^2(R) + v_{\text{gas}}^2(R) + v_{\text{halo}}^2(R)\]
Explore the interactive model on our Galactic Rotation Simulation page.

title: Lectures 21–22: Rotation Curves, Dark Matter & Spiral Arms
text:
2. Toomre Stability Criterion (\(Q\))
For a thin, rotating disk of stars or gas to resist local axisymmetric gravitational collapse, thermal velocity dispersion and differential rotation must overcome self-gravity: \[Q = \frac{\sigma_R \kappa}{3.36 \, G \, \Sigma}\] where: - \(\sigma_R\): Radial velocity dispersion of stars - \(\kappa\): Epicyclic frequency, \(\kappa^2 = R \frac{d\Omega^2}{dR} + 4\Omega^2\) - \(\Sigma\): Disk surface mass density

Stability Regimes:

\(Q < 1\): Disk is unstable to local axisymmetric gravitational collapse (forms clumps, starbursts).
\(Q > 1\): Disk is stable against axisymmetric modes.
Typically, spiral disks maintain \(Q \approx 1.2 - 2.0\), permitting non-axisymmetric spiral density waves.

title: Lectures 21–22: Rotation Curves, Dark Matter & Spiral Arms
text:
3. Lin-Shu Density Wave Theory
Spiral arms are not material structures (which would suffer the winding dilemma in differential rotation \(\Omega(R)\)), but rather quasi-stationary density waves rotating at pattern speed \(\Omega_p\).
The dispersion relation for tightly wound spiral waves is: \[(\omega - m\Omega)^2 = \kappa^2 - 2\pi G \Sigma |k| + k^2 c_s^2\] where \(m\) is the number of arms and \(k\) is the radial wavenumber.
Resonances occur where pattern speed matches orbital or epicyclic frequencies: - Corotation Resonance (CR): \(\Omega(R) = \Omega_p\) - Inner Lindblad Resonance (ILR): \(\Omega(R) - \kappa(R)/m = \Omega_p\) - Outer Lindblad Resonance (OLR): \(\Omega(R) + \kappa(R)/m = \Omega_p\)
